intro: The third movement of Berg’s Lyric Suite has a Trio estatico between two statements of the Allegro misterioso. The Galimir Quartet of Vienna played it on a set issued in the United States as Brunswick-Polydor BP No. 2 by March 1937.

sections.label: A′ · Allegro misterioso returns
sections.mNote: The opening music is presented backwards.

cues.title: Allegro misterioso and the A–B–H–F motif
cues.text: The movement opens with the Allegro misterioso. Berg uses the signature motif A–B♭–B♮–F, in German notation A–B–H–F, the initials of Alban Berg and Hanna Fuchs-Robettin. The motif is most prominent in this movement.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia, “Lyric Suite (Berg)”, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyric_Suite_(Berg): Berg used the signature motif A–B–H–F to combine Alban Berg and Hanna Fuchs-Robettin, “most prominent in the third movement”, after Perle’s discovery of the annotated score.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two dedications
cues.text: The published score is dedicated to Alexander Zemlinsky. Berg also dedicated the suite secretly to Hanna Fuchs-Robettin, Franz Werfel’s sister, with whom he had a love affair in the 1920s. Research by George Perle and Douglass Green uncovered it in the 1970s.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: research by Perle and Green “uncovered a long and passionate love affair” between Berg and Hanna Fuchs-Robettin, and the Lyric Suite was secretly dedicated to her. Wikipedia, “Lyric Suite (Berg)”, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyric_Suite_(Berg): the public dedication to Zemlinsky.

cues.title: Trio estatico
cues.text: The Trio estatico, the ecstatic middle section, begins. Unlike the outer sections, it is through-composed.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia, “Lyric Suite (Berg)”, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyric_Suite_(Berg): the third movement is an ABA form in which “the Trio estatico, the B section of the ABA, is through-composed”.

cues.title: Return, played backwards
cues.text: The Allegro misterioso returns. In the outer sections Berg presents the same music forwards and then backwards, so the reprise runs the opening material in reverse.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia, “Lyric Suite (Berg)”, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyric_Suite_(Berg): the outer sections of the Allegro misterioso “present the same music forwards and then backwards”. Douglas Jarman, Musicologica Austriaca (2017), https://www.musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/pdf/34 : the two parts of the Allegro misterioso are related as a retrograde, and Berg’s annotated score marks the start of the retrograde “Vergessen Sie es”.

cues.title: The Galimir Quartet
cues.text: The Galimir Quartet of Vienna consisted of a brother and three sisters. Louis Krasner heard them play the Lyric Suite in Vienna in early 1935, fell in love with the second violinist, Adrienne Galimir, and married her.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: Krasner heard the Galimir Quartet play the Lyric Suite in Vienna early in 1935 and “fell in love with, proposed to, and married Adrienne Galimir, the second violinist in the quartet, which then consisted of a brother and three sisters”.

cues.title: The American issue, 1937
cues.text: The suite appeared in the United States on Brunswick-Polydor as set BP No. 2, advertised in March 1937 alongside Stravinsky’s Violin Concerto with Samuel Dushkin and Roussel’s Third Symphony.
cues.evidence: The American Music Lover, vol. 2 no. 11, March 1937, Brunswick-Polydor advertisement listing, among others, Sets BP No. 1 (Stravinsky, Dushkin), No. 2 (Berg, Galimir Quartet) and No. 3 (Roussel, Wolff): https://archive.org/details/sim_american-record-guide_1937-03_2_11

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Felix Galimir (violin I), Adrienne Galimir (spelled “Adrielle” in the item description) (violin II), Renée Galimir (viola), Marguerite Galimir (cello)
fields.note: The advertisement names the “Galimir String Quartet of Vienna”. The item description lists the four players. The second violinist’s name is “Adrielle” there and Adrienne in the Boston Symphony Orchestra note, which says the quartet consisted of a brother and three sisters.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Berg’s Lyric Suite for string quartet (the 1926 quartet version); the edition used by the performers is not stated.
fields.note: The Internet Archive description gives the title and “for string quartet (1926)”; the advertisement of 1937 gives “Suite Lyrique. For String Quartet”. The movement is the third of six; the file runs 3:42 and carries the whole movement.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Stated in the item description (“Recorded c. 1935-36”). Wikipedia’s list of recordings gives “ca. 1935”; no session ledger was seen.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Stated in the item description, which says the recording was made “for French Polydor”. The label of the American disc 95007 reads “Recorded in France”.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The item description lists the three issues and adds a reissue by Vox in July 1948. The March 1937 advertisement shows the American issue by Brunswick-Polydor.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Brunswick-Polydor set BP No. 2 (records 95006–95009; slide-automatic set BP-2A, 95010–95013); earlier issues Polydor 516.659–516.662 and Decca CA-8244–8247 as given in the item description
fields.note: The set number BP No. 2 is confirmed by the March 1937 advertisement and by the label photograph of disc 95007; the Polydor and Decca numbers and the British issue date (December 1936) are from the item description only. Wikipedia’s list of recordings gives the first issue as Polydor 595.135–595.138; the two sets of numbers were not reconciled.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Brunswick-Polydor 95007, “In 8 Parts”, Part III, with the third movement named on the label; matrix and take numbers are not given
fields.note: Read from the label photograph in the Internet Archive item (“Part III … Set No. BP-2 … Third Movement: Allegro misterioso”). The item description and the label give no matrix or take numbers. The files are labelled (i) to (vi), one for each movement.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Internet Archive collection shellackophile-recordings; no individual transfer credit
fields.note: The item names a collection but no transfer engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.value: Not stated; the item was made public on 13 March 2022
fields.note: The public date of the item is an upload date, not the date of the transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Each movement is one file, uploaded as FLAC with an MP3 derivative; equalisation and noise reduction are not described.
fields.note: The published MP3 is the Internet Archive derivative.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Berg died in 1935, so the work has been in the public domain in the EU and other life-plus-70 countries since 2006. Its United States status is not assessed here.
fields.note: Rights in the composition are stated separately from rights in the recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first published before 1963; the American issue was advertised by March 1937.
fields.note: The item description gives earlier French and British issues, which were not checked in a second source. The United States status of a recording made in France in the 1930s is not established.

dossier.credit: Alban Berg, Lyric Suite, III. Galimir String Quartet of Vienna. Recorded c. 1935–36; issued as Brunswick-Polydor set BP No. 2, advertised in March 1937. Internet Archive item bp-2-berg-suite-lyrique-iv (collection shellackophile-recordings). Territorial EU basis (first published before 1963); US status not established.

composer.epithet: Composer of Wozzeck, an opera about an exploited soldier, and of a twelve-note concerto that quotes a Bach chorale and is dedicated to the memory of Manon Gropius.
facts: Vienna; a summer house by the Wörthersee from 1932
Violin Concerto, 1935; commissioned by Louis Krasner, dedicated to Manon Gropius
composer.background:
In 1904 Berg’s brother Charly secretly took some of Alban’s songs to Arnold Schoenberg. Their sister Smaragda had spotted an advertisement for lessons in harmony and counterpoint. Alban was nineteen, a bookseller’s son from Vienna, writing songs and working in the civil service. His father had died four years earlier, and there was little money for tuition. Schoenberg accepted him all the same, though he could not pay the fee. Recalling their first meeting in a recording made in 1949, Schoenberg described “a very tall youngster and extremely timid”, whose songs stood stylistically between Hugo Wolf and Brahms.

An inheritance in 1906 allowed Berg to leave the office. When his mother proposed the conservatoire, Schoenberg heard, he wept until she agreed he could stay with his teacher. Lessons lasted until 1910. The Piano Sonata, Op. 1, completed in 1908, shows Schoenberg’s developing variation at work: small phrases change and grow, through whole-tone passages to a final B minor. The String Quartet, Op. 3, shares its themes between two movements; its opening idea returns near the close.
